title: Resistance, Hiding, and the Struggle to Survive in Łuków
summary: The records show that Łuków Jews resisted in the ghetto and forests, sought refuge in hiding places, and faced danger even beyond the German occupation.

## A resistance assembled under siege

In the memorial book’s account, resistance in Łuków was not a single uprising with one agreed plan. It was a dangerous, improvised effort: people gathered weapons, organized fighters, smuggled food, sought refuge, and tried to escape toward the forests. The book’s chapters preserve accounts from different witnesses, written from different vantage points. They do not always settle how many groups there were, who commanded them, or what happened to every fighter.

The town’s [Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_be37822e0d02ca035148a5dc) faced the German occupation in a region where deportation and mass murder had become an immediate threat. The [Łuków ghetto](/communities/lukow/records/mention_76301e2ac4606782b1048c9c) held local Jews and people driven there from elsewhere. Yad Vashem’s ghetto encyclopedia provides a wider chronology: it records the ghetto’s population rising to about 10,000 by May 1942, the deportations and killings of October and November, and a remaining population of several hundred legally registered Jews alongside more than a thousand who had evaded deportation. The figures and categories in such accounts describe a changing, violently disrupted population, not a stable census. ([Yad Vashem, “Łuków”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

The memorial book places the weapons effort in 1943. A group of “reliable people,” it says, decided to collect arms in the ghetto in preparation for a final battle. Among those named are [Yekhiel Anshtak](/communities/lukow/records/mention_a46556c9d8d4055f4065ee12), [Reuven Weisboim](/communities/lukow/records/mention_f3bc4e03dbe04f2d4356ecd8), [Sholem Walowski](/communities/lukow/records/mention_2871f334811e3caa4d737015), [Avraham Lichtenstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_165ca2876954b897ad23cea9), [Berek Feferman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_eeeffb8c41650d54b4b236ce), [Yosl Biderman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_8b3a7fac6fc915889b3c9720), [Hersh Mendl Goldenberg](/communities/lukow/records/mention_83253594fadf48992440b16d), [Leyb Barenstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_9c564173783ca6db2d42ac28), and the [Fridman brothers](/communities/lukow/records/mention_7e30ad0ed396b8ba46b5e465). It also identifies [Mendl Lentshner](/communities/lukow/records/mention_ade6f5f5e359174dcfe6f283) as their father. These are names in the memorial book’s testimony; the supplied records do not provide a full account of each person’s family or fate.

## Arms, couriers, and the forest

The book describes weapons as more than a means of fighting inside the ghetto. Its separate chapter on an early search for arms and its partisan narratives point toward the difficult connection between ghetto resistance and escape. The supplied record names [Pesakh Goldenberg](/communities/lukow/records/mention_d412fc994923e7073cccca41) as an intermediary who helped smuggle weapons in. [Pesakh Shneymer](/communities/lukow/records/mention_9c0c1119cacf2421f1ad201d) is remembered as bringing weapons into the ghetto and falling while fighting the Gestapo. The evidence provided does not make clear the precise date, location, or sequence of that final encounter.

The book also recalls [Poliak Novimsky](/communities/lukow/records/mention_5ca280b70ea51ad45ef75de9), a former Łuków pharmacist, organizing two Jewish combat groups. In another account, survivors gathered as fighters in a forest near Łuków under Anshtak and Weisboim; the passage is incomplete, so the group’s size and its actions cannot be reconstructed confidently from that fragment alone. The memorial volume’s chapter titles—“Łuków Partisans in the Belorussian Forests” and “Memoirs from a Jewish Partisan Troop”—show that forest fighting and partisan life formed an important part of the community’s remembered story. They do not, by themselves, establish that every fighter named in the ghetto accounts joined the same unit.

Independent context helps explain the peril and purpose of these preparations. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that in smaller ghettos, arms could be vital for escape: some partisan groups would not accept Jewish fugitives without weapons, while resistance inside a ghetto might buy time for people to flee. It also describes the barriers—scarcity of weapons, hunger, fear of collective reprisals, and the danger to families—that constrained action. This is a regional framework, not evidence that every motive or circumstance applied to every Łuków fighter. ([USHMM, “Resistance in the Smaller Ghettos of Eastern Europe”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/resistance-in-the-smaller-ghettos-of-eastern-europe))

Yad Vashem’s Łuków account independently records an underground group of about fifteen members, led by Moshe Vishni, organizing in late 1942 or early 1943. It says the group escaped and joined partisans in the area. That account differs in names and leadership from the memorial book’s reports of Novimsky’s two groups and the Anshtak–Weisboim forest regrouping. The available evidence does not show whether these are different stages or groups, variant names, or accounts that overlap. They should not be collapsed into one supposedly certain organization. ([Yad Vashem, “Łuków”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

## Food, refuge, and the risks beyond the ghetto

Resistance also meant keeping people alive from day to day. The memorial book remembers [Reuven Weisboim](/communities/lukow/records/mention_f3bc4e03dbe04f2d4356ecd8) as repeatedly risking his life to gather food for starving Jews in the ghetto. That account places clandestine aid beside armed preparation: food smuggling did not look like combat, but it confronted the deprivation imposed on the community and exposed the courier to grave danger.

Other testimonies describe flight and concealment as uncertain, temporary choices rather than guaranteed rescue. One narrator followed a woman and a girl through an attic route to a hiding place. Another recalls hiding with two boys in hay in a barn for several months. During an Aktion, German and Ukrainian searchers looked through ruined houses for people in hiding. The fragments do not identify all the narrators or the exact locations, so the experiences should not be assigned to particular named fighters without further evidence.

The risks did not end once someone crossed the ghetto boundary. The memorial book records the murder of a narrator’s mother and brother by Poles in a village near the end of 1943. It also recalls the murder of the Kesselbrener family after they had been hidden in Domina. In another account, armed Poles murdered Jewish youths who had accepted an offer to fight the Germans alongside them. These are specific testimonies about particular events; they should not be turned into a claim about every local inhabitant or every partisan group. They do, however, make clear why seeking shelter or joining fighters could involve dangers from multiple directions.

The account by [Elijah Rodziniak](/communities/lukow/records/mention_fbed85a1da78469e4970f4ff) brings the choices back to family. His mother remained among the Jews in the ghetto, while his testimony describes escape efforts in 1943. The supplied evidence does not resolve her fate or establish the full route of his flight. That gap matters: a memorial book assembled by survivors can preserve extraordinary detail while still leaving relatives, neighbors, and people who died elsewhere beyond its reach.

## What the record can—and cannot—settle

Yad Vashem records that on May 2, 1943, German forces burned the ghetto, killed some residents at the Jewish cemetery, and deported others to Treblinka; only a few succeeded in escaping to the forests. This provides an outside chronological frame for the final catastrophe. The memorial book’s accounts, by contrast, give names and remembered acts—arming, carrying food, finding hiding places, and trying to reach the forest—that institutional summaries cannot supply. ([Yad Vashem, “Łuków”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529))

Together, the sources resist a simple distinction between “fighters” and “survivors.” A person might help collect weapons, smuggle food, flee, hide, or try to reach a partisan unit; these were connected responses to a campaign of destruction, not interchangeable paths to safety. The memorial book preserves disagreements and incomplete fragments rather than a single comprehensive roster. Its testimony should be read with that limitation in view—and with attention to the people it does name.

The route from Łuków to the forests, the identity of the groups led by Novimsky, Anshtak, and Weisboim, and the fate of the young men approached by armed Poles remain important questions for further research. So do the identities behind Domina and the village where Rodziniak’s mother and brother were killed. The surviving record is not the whole story; it is a starting point for recovering lives and relationships that the violence scattered.
